claim: Against a labelled 47-payload corpus, the hired scanner's decision-level recall — the share of the labelled attacks it did not leave at ALLOW — exceeds the stated keyword list's, and its decision-level precision exceeds flag_everything's, which is the corpus base rate.
falsifier: If the hired scanner's decision-level recall does not exceed keyword_match's, or its decision-level precision does not exceed flag_everything's (the corpus base rate), the claim is refuted and the report says so.

metric.formula: Class level, for each class C in the corpus's nine-code label vocabulary: recall(C) = |payloads labelled C whose returned threat_classes contain C| / |payloads labelled C|; precision(C) = |payloads returning C that are labelled C| / |payloads returning C|. Overall class-level recall = |attack payloads for which at least one of that payload's labelled classes was returned| / |attack payloads scored|. Decision level, where an attack is caught when verdict != "ALLOW": recall = |attack payloads with verdict != ALLOW| / |attack payloads scored|; precision = |attack payloads with verdict != ALLOW| / |all payloads with verdict != ALLOW|. Every denominator is scored payloads — those with at least one successful scan — and never the corpus size; a payload with zero successful scans is excluded from every numerator and every denominator and is listed by payload_id, and n_failed_scans and n_payloads_unscored are reported beside every rate. Every rate is {numerator, denominator, value} and value is null when the denominator is 0. CORPUS_MATCH and STATISTICAL_ANOMALY are outside the label vocabulary because they describe how the scanner reached a detection rather than anything an attacker writes: an emission of either is never a class-level match and never a class-level false positive, and does count at decision level because it moves the verdict. A payload's scored result is its first successful trial of the three passes; passes disagreeing with it on the verdict or on the set of threat_classes are counted and reported as n_payloads_unstable with their payload ids.
metric.name: class_and_decision_precision_recall

null_baselines.name: flag_nothing
null_baselines.what_it_does: Returns verdict ALLOW and no threat classes for every payload in the corpus. Computed by docket.advantage.v2.scoring.flag_nothing and scored by the same score() that scores the hire.
null_baselines.why_it_is_the_right_null: The floor: doing nothing at all. Its recall is 0 by construction and its precision has a denominator of zero, because an arm that never flags is never wrong when it flags. That is exactly why every rate here is reported as {numerator, denominator, value} with a null value rather than as a float — a division would hand a scanner that caught nothing a perfect precision.

null_baselines.name: flag_everything
null_baselines.what_it_does: Returns verdict BLOCK and no threat classes for every payload in the corpus. Computed by docket.advantage.v2.scoring.flag_everything and scored by the same score() that scores the hire.
null_baselines.why_it_is_the_right_null: Its decision-level recall is 1 and its decision-level precision is the corpus base rate — 31 hostile payloads of 47 — so it states how much precision is available for free to an arm that reads nothing and blocks everyone. A scanner's precision is evidence of discrimination only in as much as it exceeds that line. It names no class, which is the second thing it shows: flagging and naming the class are different work, and only the first is free.

null_baselines.name: keyword_match
null_baselines.what_it_does: Flags a payload when any term in the registered list appears in its text, case-insensitively, as a plain substring, and returns ALLOW otherwise. It emits a flag only and no threat classes, so it participates at the decision level only and no class mapping is invented for it. Computed by docket.advantage.v2.scoring.keyword_match. The list is carried verbatim in this record's `keywords` field, in the order it was registered.
null_baselines.why_it_is_the_right_null: The hire is worth its price only against the cheapest thing a caller could write instead, and that is a word list. Its limitation is stated rather than hidden: the keyword list was written by the same hand that authored the corpus, so it is a neutral-to-optimistic null and not an adversarial one. A reader who thinks it is too weak can re-run scoring.py with their own list against the published corpus, which is why the two travel together.

question: Does the hired scanner flag a larger share of labelled attacks than the stated keyword list while keeping enough precision to exceed an arm that flags everything?
stopping_rule: Three passes over every payload in the corpus, once. No payload is re-scanned because its result was unwelcome, and no payload was edited after its scan was seen.
